catalog_locator: Ch. 5 'The Hainan Cham sound system': sec. 5.1 Word structure and sec. 5.5 Tones (Google Books ebook pages PT47, PT50, PT51; print p. 36ff), plus ch. 1 sec. 1.2 'Convergence Under Contact' (PT24). re-.
catalog_quote: [5.1 Word structure] HC is now largely monosyllabic, although forms with more than one syllable occur. In contrast, the earliest Proto-Chamic (PC) forms were overwhelmingly disyllabic. It can be argued that the tendency toward monosyllabification began at the PC level with the switch from initial to final stress in disyllabic forms. However, it is hard to argue that the process was totally unaffected by intense contact with the monosyllabic languages of Hainan. ... [5.5 Tones] All synchronic analyses of HC agree that it has five phonemic tones (Ouyang and Zheng 1983; Ni Dabai 1988ab, 1990ab; Maddieson and Peng 1993; Zheng 1997; Thurgood and Thurgood 2005). There are, however, differences in labeling, which we discuss below. ... The five phonemic tones used in this work together with examples are given in Table 6. ... [Table 6: 55, 33, 21, 43, 24] ... Tones 24 and 43 are invariably contour tones. Tone 24 is a low-rising tone. Tone 43 is a high-falling tone. ... [5.6] HC is the only fully tonal Chamic language. ... [1.2] In terms of phonology, HC has restructured from a sesquisyllabic, iambically stressed, atonal (although probably marginally registral) language to a monosyllabic, fully tonal language. New phonemes have also been added under the influence of the languages of Hainan.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Tsat/Hainan Cham is a largely monosyllabic, fully tonal language with five phonemic tones (55, 33, 21, 43, 24); the grammar makes no synchronic word-stress statement. Stress figures only in the history: Proto-Malayo-Chamic penultimate stress > Proto-Chamic final (iambic) stress > loss of the presyllable > Tsat monosyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Polysyllabic forms exist (mostly loans/compounds) but no prominence pattern is described for them; sec. 5.5 notes limited tone sandhi (three examples from Ouyang & Zheng 1983: 32-33), two classifiers whose 55 tone varies with 21, and that 'final particles often have a neutral tone rather than their basic tone'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level (lexical tone on every syllable; citation forms). Phrase-level focus prosody is treated separately by Wang et al. 2012 (no post-focus compression).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Tsat = Hainan Cham (HC) = Utsat = Huihui(hua) 回辉话, spoken in Huihui and Huixin villages, Yanglan township, Sanya, Hainan (Glottolog tsat1238, ISO huq). The 2014 grammar and the 2005 chapter rest on Zheng 1997 plus the authors' 2004 fieldwork (6 speakers).

new_statements.quote: Phonologically, Northern Roglai is sesquisyllabic and atonal whereas Hainan Cham is monosyllabic and fully tonal. [...] Essentially, when the language that was to become Hainan Cham arrived on the island, it was sesquisyllabic–a weakly stressed onset syllable followed by a stressed main syllable; under the influence of the tonal languages of Hainan, it became monosyllabic and tonal–Modern Hainan Cham has a rich, 5-way tonal system. However, this restructuring of the phonology of Hainan Cham has been written about extensively elsewhere and there is no reason to go into it further here (Haudricourt 1984, Benedict 1984, Maddieson and Pang 1993, Ni 1988ab, 1990ab Thurgood 1993, 1996, 1999, Thurgood and Thurgood in press (instrumental)).

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Thurgood, Thurgood & Li 2014 (tone language, now largely monosyllabic, earlier switch to final stress at the Proto-Chamic level): both say the modern language is tonal with no stress rule and that the ancestor had final (main-syllable) stress. Read from the author's preprint, not the published Brill text; wording may differ slightly in print.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Hainan Cham is described as monosyllabic and fully tonal (five tones); no synchronic word-stress rule is given. The only stress remark is diachronic: the pre-Hainan ancestor was sesquisyllabic with a weakly stressed presyllable followed by the stressed main (final) syllable, i.e. iambic/final stress, which was lost with monosyllabification and tonogenesis.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the paper is a sociolinguistic contact study and explicitly defers phonological detail to Thurgood 1993, 1996, 1999 and Thurgood & Thurgood 2005
new_statements.identity_note: Both listed works concern Hainan Cham (= Tsat / Utsat, ISO huq) of Huihui and Huixin villages near Sanya, Hainan; the 2010 paper also treats Anong (Tibeto-Burman) and Phan Rang / Eastern Cham (Vietnam), which are separate languages and were not used for this compilation. The earlier catalog quote comes from Thurgood, Thurgood & Li 2014, the same variety.

new_statements.rule_in_words: From snippets only: the book treats Tsat (Hainan Cham) as a Chamic language that, under contact with the monosyllabic (tonal) languages of Hainan, moved from iambic (final-stressed sesquisyllabic) word shape to monosyllables and developed tones (index: 'Tsat.. development of tones, 214-232'); the only word-stress statement visible is the family-level Proto-Chamic shift to final-syllable stress under Mon-Khmer influence (pp. 60-62). No synchronic word-stress rule for Tsat is visible in the snippets; the full Tsat tone chapter could not be read.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsat / Utsat / Hainan Cham (Huihui speech of the Hui villages Huihui and Huixin near Sanya, Hainan); Thurgood 1999 treats it under the name Tsat, subgrouped with Northern Roglai.
